clinicalPearls: A common, self-limiting cause of neonatal respiratory distress from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid
Typically presents soon after birth with tachypnoea, mild recession and grunting in a near-term or term baby
Elective caesarean birth without labour is a major risk factor, as is late prematurity and maternal diabetes
It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, with infection and other causes of distress ruled out
Chest radiography classically shows prominent perihilar streaking and fluid in the horizontal fissure
Management is supportive with oxygen and respiratory support as needed, and it usually resolves within a day or two
reference.pathophysiology: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn results from delayed absorption of the fluid that normally fills the fetal lungs. During labour and vaginal birth, hormonal changes and thoracic compression promote clearance of this fluid via epithelial sodium channels and the lymphatics; when this process is incomplete, as after caesarean birth without labour, residual fluid in the airspaces and interstitium impairs gas exchange and reduces compliance, producing tachypnoea and mild distress. As the fluid is reabsorbed over hours to a couple of days, the symptoms resolve.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of respiratory rate, effort and oxygenation
Chest radiograph showing perihilar streaking and fissural fluid
Sepsis screen where infection cannot be excluded
Blood gas to assess gas exchange
Pre- and post-ductal saturations if pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease is considered
redFlags: Worsening or persistent distress beyond the expected short course
Hypoxaemia out of proportion suggesting pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving within one to three days with supportive care and no long-term respiratory sequelae.
pitfalls: Attributing distress to TTN and missing early sepsis or pneumonia
Overlooking a cardiac cause of persistent hypoxaemia
Assuming resolution without reassessing worsening distress
Failing to recognise persistent pulmonary hypertension
management: Supportive care with supplemental oxygen and non-invasive respiratory support such as continuous positive airway pressure, titrated to the infant's oxygen requirement
Provide nasogastric or intravenous nutrition and fluids while tachypnoea precludes safe oral feeding
Monitor respiratory rate, effort, oxygenation and blood gas, using pre- and post-ductal saturations to help exclude pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease
Screen for infection and cover empirically with antibiotics until sepsis and pneumonia are excluded, as it is a diagnosis of exclusion
Provide parental reassurance and expect spontaneous resolution within one to three days as foetal lung fluid is reabsorbed
Escalate to neonatal intensive care and reconsider alternative diagnoses if respiratory distress worsens or fails to settle as expected
